doc.title: Jackie Cain and Roy Kral interviewed by Monk Rowe, New York City, New York, March 22, 1998

chapter: Studio notes, hits and old friends
title: Hit records, albums, and revisiting old songs
summary: Their hits and what a jazz hit meant, the Free and Easy and all-star big-band albums, and now reviving old tunes in a lower key.

story.theme_name: In the studio: making records, then and now
story.community_name: Record labels, producers and the business of making albums

blocks.x: And you had a couple of really good records in those years with Ventura?
Yeah we had “East of Suez,” we had “Euphoria,” “I’m Forever Blowing Bubbles,” and then after we left Ventura we got into having a mini-hit with “Mountain Greenery,” and that was kind of wonderful.
What does a hit in the jazz world translate to in record sales?
Possibly in the top ten of the jazz choices for the week. I think you can only find it in DownBeat magazine.
And as far as sales go, I don’t think we know anything about that, we’d have to ask Creed Taylor or somebody.

But we’ve been very fortunate we feel because we’ve had an opportunity to do different albums with little different flavors to them. Like one time we did an album with about a 14 piece band, that was called “Free and Easy,” and that was a great thing. It was all Bill Holman charts, and that was different from the big band album that we did which was about 18 pieces, which had, it was an all-star band. I mean it had Clark Terry, Art Farmer, Phil Woods — no I don’t know if it was Phil.

But, yeah I think it was. Gene Quill, all these great, great players that we were so honored to be able to work with, and just even having Quincy write and all these people that wrote for it, it was a thrill for us to be able to do that. Because that’s what it’s all about you know, about doing something new. And people sort of like one thing that they’ve heard and they get attached to it, and they want you to do it all the time. You know like we don’t do “I’m Forever Blowing Bubbles” anymore really, and we don’t do “Mountain Greenery,” except that this year being our fiftieth anniversary we decided it was a smart thing to do it, and we were not sick of it anymore. I mean when you do it again after you haven’t done it after a number of years—
Well there’s another thing to it. On “Mountain Greenery” we discovered that, well I for one, I can’t sing that high anymore.

Well it’s harder for him too because he’s playing and singing you know, and it’s harder to do it. I can make it but some of them are a strain, you know, some of the high notes. But we did put “Cheerful Little Earful” down a half — a half or a whole step.
Anyway it doesn’t matter. But we made it a little lower because we couldn’t sing it that high anymore.
